COLLEGE OF EDUCATION MISSION 
The mission of DePaul University's College of Education is to prepare educators, counselors, and leaders who are committed to creating equitable, compassionate, intellectually rich, and socially just environments. As part of a Vincentian university, we cultivate the social conscience, understandings, and practices necessary to address social inequities among and with individuals, communities, and institutions. We develop critical, creative, knowledgeable practitioners and scholars who continually inquire and reflect on educational and professional practices. Through authentic experiences in and outside the classroom and other educational environments we prepare our students to be engaged, service- oriented citizens of local and global communities.


PROGRAM PERFORMANCE STANDARDS 
Both the state and the DePaul College of Education expect you to meet performance standards. Program Standards can be found at https://education.depaul.edu/student-resources/policies-and-forms/Pages/program-standards.aspx

Life was full of interest for Rosamunda - usually called Ros for short.
The friends, the sights, the smells, the never-ending games, and the snow, that wonderful frozen cotton wool, to bounce through. Life had been filled with one enjoyable adventure after another - until the last one!
It had not been an adventure of Ros's making. She had no say in the matter. When the family moved house she would naturally go with them; with the house-proud mother who could crochet anything from evening gowns to the woolly mammoth Ros played with, and the father (not so much fun) who was very important in the city and, unfortunately, all too aware of the fact. And, of course, they would be accompanied by their children; Peter, cropped hair like the bristles of a startled hedgehog and impish grin, and Amanda, well-behaved, considerate and always ready to stop Ros chasing pigeons. Despite this, Ros still liked her.
The new, huge house was intended to meet their father's aspirations, if no anyone else's. The rest of the family had been happy in their suburban semi only a 10 minute walk to school, two minutes to their grandmother and with a nearby tube station. It would have been the closest thing to living in the countryside if it hadn't been for the other houses blocking the view. When spring came the cherry trees lining the wide avenue blossomed and collared doves tried to nest in their apple tree (Ros's incessant barking always ensured they never succeeded). Everyone went to the park wearing summer clothes, only to dash the short distance back home to put on coats when they realised how cold it was, and the powder-puff seeds of early dandelions alighted on the nearby allotments. The beans, peas, tomatoes, artichokes and cauliflowers growing there would be sold from stalls at the gates later in the year to undercut the overpriced produce in the local supermarket.
Why would Ros's family want to move from this suburban idyll, two minutes from the park and boating lake, to a huge house in the middle of nowhere surrounded by farms owned by people with guns ready to eliminate sheep worrying dogs? As soon as the removal van arrived, Ros had the foreboding that this was going to be no fun at all. She was convinced that their new neighbours would shoot first before wondering whether the innocent, fluffy mongrel passing by their fields was someone's pet. Not that Ros had ever been fluffy, more a cross between a poodle and bottlebrush.
The drive out seemed to take forever. 
Ros watched dolefully from the back of the hatchback with Peter and Amanda as suburbia disappeared. They entered a maze of country lanes which wound through a patchwork of fields filled with startling yellow and the intense green of immature wheat. Ros thought she glimpsed circling buzzards, probably over a sheep carcass, but tried not to think about it.
As they entered some rusty wrought iron gates all the misgivings the reluctant family had were confirmed. How could any corner of the idyllic English countryside be so foreboding?
The house at the end of the overgrown drive was Victorian Gothic, from front porch to forbidding rear courtyard. Its hall should have been filled with mediaeval armour and mounted heads of any creatures unfortunate enough to be found by the local farmers near a field of their sheep. Peter and Amanda were not impressed. Having left all their friends behind, they were hardly consoled by their father's offhand insistence that they could still keep in contact through Facebook. This from the man whose idea of socialising was working lunches with other bankers. He could not comprehend how fraught the online world could be for the discerning young mind. Peter preferred to play football outside anyway and not on some stupid games console, let alone chat to Mike, Tyrone and Ali - who would now be in the park kicking a ball around - on a social networking site. And where in this wilderness was he liable to find enough friends to make up a five-a-side team? 
Amanda had closed her Facebook account when a troll started to leave offensive messages on the get well page she had set up for a schoolfriend being treated with cancer. Some flowers and a card had been far more appreciated anyway. Apart from that, their father had moved them to the middle of somewhere which didn't even have a decent broadband signal. This didn't matter to him because he was always in the City and used his smartphone. That could always get a connection. He had isolated his own family from the world they knew for the sake of raising his profile at the bank and golf club.

The friends, the sights, the smells, the never-ending games, and the snow, that wonderful frozen cotton wool, to bounce through. Life had been filled with one enjoyable adventure after another - until the last one!

And, of course, they would be accompanied by their children; Peter, cropped hair like the bristles of a startled hedgehog and impish grin, and Amanda, well-behaved, considerate and always ready to stop Ros chasing pigeons. Despite this, Ros still liked her.
The new, huge house was intended to meet their father's aspirations, if no anyone else's. The rest of the family had been happy in their suburban semi only a 10 minute walk to school, two minutes to their grandmother and with a nearby tube station. It would have been the closest thing to living in the countryside if it hadn't been for the other houses blocking the view. When spring came the cherry trees lining the wide avenue blossomed and collared doves tried to nest in their apple tree (Ros's incessant barking always ensured they never succeeded). Everyone went to the park wearing summer clothes, only to dash the short distance back home to put on coats when they realised how cold it was, and the powder-puff seeds of early dandelions alighted on the nearby allotments. The beans, peas, tomatoes, artichokes and cauliflowers growing there would be sold from stalls at the gates later in the year to undercut the overpriced produce in the local supermarket.
Why would Ros's family want to move from this suburban idyll, two minutes from the park and boating lake, to a huge house in the middle of nowhere surrounded by farms owned by people with guns ready to eliminate sheep worrying dogs? As soon as the removal van arrived, Ros had the foreboding that this was going to be no fun at all. She was convinced that their new neighbours would shoot first before wondering whether the innocent, fluffy mongrel passing by their fields was someone's pet. Not that Ros had ever been fluffy, more a cross between a poodle and bottlebrush.
The drive out seemed to take forever. 
Ros watched dolefully from the back of the hatchback with Peter and Amanda as suburbia disappeared. They entered a maze of country lanes which wound through a patchwork of fields filled with startling yellow and the intense green of immature wheat. Ros thought she glimpsed circling buzzards, probably over a sheep carcass, but tried not to think about it.

Its hall should have been filled with mediaeval armour and mounted heads of any creatures unfortunate enough to be found by the local farmers near a field of their sheep. Life was full of interest for Rosamunda - usually called Ros for short.
The friends, the sights, the smells, the never-ending games, and the snow, that wonderful frozen cotton wool, to bounce through. Life had been filled with one enjoyable adventure after another - until the last one!
It had not been an adventure of Ros's making. She had no say in the matter. When the family moved house she would naturally go with them; with the house-proud mother who could crochet anything from evening gowns to the woolly mammoth Ros played with, and the father (not so much fun) who was very important in the city and, unfortunately, all too aware of the fact. And, of course, they would be accompanied by their children; Peter, cropped hair like the bristles of a startled hedgehog and impish grin, and Amanda, well-behaved, considerate and always ready to stop Ros chasing pigeons. Despite this, Ros still liked her.
The new, huge house was intended to meet their father's aspirations, if no anyone else's. The rest of the family had been happy in their suburban semi only a 10 minute walk to school, two minutes to their grandmother and with a nearby tube station. It would have been the closest thing to living in the countryside if it hadn't been for the other houses blocking the view. When spring came the cherry trees lining the wide avenue blossomed and collared doves tried to nest in their apple tree (Ros's incessant barking always ensured they never succeeded). Everyone went to the park wearing summer clothes, only to dash the short distance back home to put on coats when they realised how cold it was, and the powder-puff seeds of early dandelions alighted on the nearby allotments. The beans, peas, tomatoes, artichokes and cauliflowers growing there would be sold from stalls at the gates later in the year to undercut the overpriced produce in the local supermarket.
Why would Ros's family want to move from this suburban idyll, two minutes from the park and boating lake, to a huge house in the middle of nowhere surrounded by farms owned by people with guns ready to eliminate sheep worrying dogs? As soon as the removal van arrived, Ros had the foreboding that this was going to be no fun at all. She was convinced that their new neighbours would shoot first before wondering whether the innocent, fluffy mongrel passing by their fields was someone's pet. Not that Ros had ever been fluffy, more a cross between a poodle and bottlebrush.
The drive out seemed to take forever. 
Ros watched dolefully from the back of the hatchback with Peter and Amanda as suburbia disappeared. They entered a maze of country lanes which wound through a patchwork of fields filled with startling yellow and the intense green of immature wheat. Ros thought she glimpsed circling buzzards, probably over a sheep carcass, but tried not to think about it.
As they entered some rusty wrought iron gates all the misgivings the reluctant family had were confirmed. How could any corner of the idyllic English countryside be so foreboding?
The house at the end of the overgrown drive was Victorian Gothic, from front porch to forbidding rear courtyard. Its hall should have been filled with mediaeval armour and mounted heads of any creatures unfortunate enough to be found by the local farmers near a field of their sheep. This from the man whose idea of socialising was working lunches with other bankers. He could not comprehend how fraught the online world could be for the discerning young mind. And where in this wilderness was he liable to find enough friends to make up a five-a-side team?

This didn't matter to him because he was always in the City and used his smartphone. That could always get a connection. Life was full of interest for Rosamunda - usually called Ros for short.
The friends, the sights, the smells, the never-ending games, and the snow, that wonderful frozen cotton wool, to bounce through. Life had been filled with one enjoyable adventure after another - until the last one!
It had not been an adventure of Ros's making. She had no say in the matter. When the family moved house she would naturally go with them; with the house-proud mother who could crochet anything from evening gowns to the woolly mammoth Ros played with, and the father (not so much fun) who was very important in the city and, unfortunately, all too aware of the fact. And, of course, they would be accompanied by their children; Peter, cropped hair like the bristles of a startled hedgehog and impish grin, and Amanda, well-behaved, considerate and always ready to stop Ros chasing pigeons. Despite this, Ros still liked her.
The new, huge house was intended to meet their father's aspirations, if no anyone else's. The rest of the family had been happy in their suburban semi only a 10 minute walk to school, two minutes to their grandmother and with a nearby tube station. It would have been the closest thing to living in the countryside if it hadn't been for the other houses blocking the view. When spring came the cherry trees lining the wide avenue blossomed and collared doves tried to nest in their apple tree (Ros's incessant barking always ensured they never succeeded). Everyone went to the park wearing summer clothes, only to dash the short distance back home to put on coats when they realised how cold it was, and the powder-puff seeds of early dandelions alighted on the nearby allotments. The beans, peas, tomatoes, artichokes and cauliflowers growing there would be sold from stalls at the gates later in the year to undercut the overpriced produce in the local supermarket.
Why would Ros's family want to move from this suburban idyll, two minutes from the park and boating lake, to a huge house in the middle of nowhere surrounded by farms owned by people with guns ready to eliminate sheep worrying dogs? As soon as the removal van arrived, Ros had the foreboding that this was going to be no fun at all. She was convinced that their new neighbours would shoot first before wondering whether the innocent, fluffy mongrel passing by their fields was someone's pet. Not that Ros had ever been fluffy, more a cross between a poodle and bottlebrush.
The drive out seemed to take forever. 
Ros watched dolefully from the back of the hatchback with Peter and Amanda as suburbia disappeared. They entered a maze of country lanes which wound through a patchwork of fields filled with startling yellow and the intense green of immature wheat. Ros thought she glimpsed circling buzzards, probably over a sheep carcass, but tried not to think about it.
As they entered some rusty wrought iron gates all the misgivings the reluctant family had were confirmed. How could any corner of the idyllic English countryside be so foreboding?
The house at the end of the overgrown drive was Victorian Gothic, from front porch to forbidding rear courtyard. Its hall should have been filled with mediaeval armour and mounted heads of any creatures unfortunate enough to be found by the local farmers near a field of their sheep. Peter and Amanda were not impressed. Having left all their friends behind, they were hardly consoled by their father's offhand insistence that they could still keep in contact through Facebook. This from the man whose idea of socialising was working lunches with other bankers. He could not comprehend how fraught the online world could be for the discerning young mind. Peter preferred to play football outside anyway and not on some stupid games console, let alone chat to Mike, Tyrone and Ali - who would now be in the park kicking a ball around - on a social networking site. And where in this wilderness was he liable to find enough friends to make up a five-a-side team? 
Amanda had closed her Facebook account when a troll started to leave offensive messages on the get well page she had set up for a schoolfriend being treated with cancer. Some flowers and a card had been far more appreciated anyway. Apart from that, their father had moved them to the middle of somewhere which didn't even have a decent broadband signal. This didn't matter to him because he was always in the City and used his smartphone. That could always get a connection. He had isolated his own family from the world they knew for the sake of raising his profile at the bank and golf club. 
Mother was even unhappier than her children, though would never admit it. As soon as the removal van arrived, Ros had the foreboding that this was going to be no fun at all. She was convinced that their new neighbours would shoot first before wondering whether the innocent, fluffy mongrel passing by their fields was someone's pet. Title: Attention Is All You Need
Authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
Venue: NeurIPS 2017

Overview
This paper introduces the Transformer, a neural sequence transduction architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms, without using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The key idea is that self-attention can model dependencies between tokens more efficiently and with greater parallelism than recurrence or convolution.

Main Contributions
- Proposes the Transformer, the first sequence-to-sequence model relying solely on attention.
- Replaces recurrence and convolution with self-attention and multi-head attention.
- Demonstrates superior machine translation performance with lower training cost.
- Establishes new state-of-the-art results on WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French translation tasks.

Key Ideas
1. Self-Attention
- Each token attends to all other tokens in the sequence.
- Enables direct modeling of long-range dependencies.
- Reduces the number of sequential operations needed during training.

2. Scaled Dot-Product Attention
- Computes attention as:
  Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
- Scaling by sqrt(d_k) prevents large dot products from causing small gradients.

3. Multi-Head Attention
- Uses multiple attention heads in parallel.
- Allows the model to attend to different representation subspaces and positions simultaneously.
- Improves expressiveness compared with a single attention mechanism.

4. Encoder-Decoder Structure
- Encoder: 6 stacked layers, each with:
  - Multi-head self-attention
  - Position-wise feed-forward network
- Decoder: 6 stacked layers, each with:
  - Masked multi-head self-attention
  - Encoder-decoder attention
  - Position-wise feed-forward network
- Residual connections and layer normalization are applied throughout.

5. Positional Encoding
- Since the model has no recurrence or convolution, token order is injected using positional encodings.
- The paper uses sinusoidal positional encodings based on sine and cosine functions of different frequencies.
- These encodings allow the model to represent relative and absolute positions.

Why the Transformer Matters
- Unlike RNNs, the Transformer allows much more parallelization during training.
- Self-attention creates shorter paths between tokens, which helps learn long-range dependencies.
- For many NLP tasks, this leads to better quality and faster training.

Results
- English-to-German (WMT 2014): 28.4 BLEU with Transformer (big), more than 2 BLEU better than previous best results.
- English-to-French (WMT 2014): 41.0 BLEU with Transformer (big), achieving state-of-the-art single-model performance.
- Training cost was significantly lower than prior top-performing systems.

Important Model Details
- Base model:
  - 6 layers
  - d_model = 512
  - d_ff = 2048
  - 8 attention heads
- Big model:
  - d_model = 1024
  - d_ff = 4096
  - 16 attention heads
- Uses Adam optimizer with a custom learning rate schedule and warmup.
- Applies dropout and label smoothing for regularization.

Strengths
- Highly parallelizable.
- Strong performance on translation benchmarks.
- More efficient than recurrent architectures.
- Attention heads provide some interpretability.

Limitations / Notes
- Self-attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length, which can be expensive for very long sequences.
- The paper suggests restricted/local attention as a future direction for long inputs.

Conclusion
The paper presents the Transformer as a major advance in sequence modeling. By relying entirely on attention, it achieves better translation performance, faster training, and greater parallelism than previous recurrent or convolution-based approaches. This work became foundational for modern NLP and large language models.

1. Main contribution
- The paper introduces the Transformer, a neural sequence transduction architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms.
- It removes recurrence and convolution, which were dominant in prior sequence models.

2. Core idea
- The model relies on self-attention to capture relationships between tokens regardless of distance.
- This design enables much greater parallelization during training compared with recurrent neural networks.

3. Architecture
- The Transformer follows an encoder-decoder structure.
- Encoder: 6 identical layers, each with multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network.
- Decoder: 6 identical layers, each with masked multi-head self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, and a feed-forward network.
- Residual connections and layer normalization are used throughout.

4. Attention mechanisms
- Scaled dot-product attention computes attention weights using query-key similarity, scaled by the square root of key dimension.
- Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, allowing the model to learn from different representation subspaces.
- The paper uses 8 heads in the base model.

5. Positional information
- Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, it adds positional encodings to token embeddings.
- The paper mainly uses sinusoidal positional encodings, which help the model represent token order and may generalize to longer sequences.

6. Why Transformer matters
- Self-attention shortens the path between distant tokens, making long-range dependencies easier to learn.
- It reduces sequential computation and improves training efficiency.
- It is especially effective for machine translation tasks.

7. Training setup
- Optimizer: Adam with a custom learning-rate schedule and warmup.
- Regularization: dropout and label smoothing.
- Trained on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French datasets.

8. Results
- Transformer (big) achieved 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German.
- Transformer (big) achieved 41.0 BLEU on English-to-French.
- These results surpassed prior state-of-the-art systems while requiring substantially less training cost.

9. Key conclusion
- Attention alone can outperform recurrent and convolutional approaches in sequence transduction.
- The Transformer became a foundational architecture for modern natural language processing.

1. Main contribution
- The paper introduces the Transformer, a sequence transduction architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms.
- It removes recurrence and convolution, which were dominant in prior sequence models.
- The design improves parallelization and reduces training time while achieving better translation quality.

2. Core idea
- The model relies on self-attention to capture dependencies between tokens regardless of distance.
- Instead of processing tokens sequentially like RNNs, the Transformer processes sequences in parallel.
- This makes it especially efficient for machine translation and other sequence modeling tasks.

3. Model architecture
- The Transformer follows an encoder-decoder structure.
- The encoder has 6 identical layers, each with:
  - multi-head self-attention
  - position-wise feed-forward networks
- The decoder also has 6 identical layers, with:
  - masked multi-head self-attention
  - encoder-decoder attention
  - position-wise feed-forward networks
- Residual connections and layer normalization are applied throughout.

4. Attention mechanisms
- Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes attention using query, key, and value vectors.
- The dot product is scaled by the square root of the key dimension to stabilize gradients.
- Multi-Head Attention uses multiple parallel attention heads so the model can learn different relationships simultaneously.
- This helps the model attend to information from different representation subspaces.

5. Positional encoding
- Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, it needs explicit position information.
- The paper adds sinusoidal positional encodings to token embeddings.
- These encodings allow the model to represent token order and generalize to longer sequences.

6. Why self-attention matters
- Self-attention reduces the number of sequential operations compared with recurrent models.
- It provides shorter paths between distant positions, making long-range dependencies easier to learn.
- For many NLP tasks, it is computationally more efficient than recurrent and convolutional alternatives.

7. Training setup
- Experiments were performed on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French translation tasks.
- Training used Adam, learning-rate warmup, dropout, and label smoothing.
- The base model trained in about 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs; the big model trained in about 3.5 days.

8. Results
- On English-to-German, Transformer (big) achieved 28.4 BLEU, improving over previous best results by more than 2 BLEU.
- On English-to-French, Transformer (big) achieved 41.0 BLEU.
- The model outperformed previous state-of-the-art systems while using a fraction of the training cost.

9. Significance
- The paper established attention as a powerful alternative to recurrence for sequence modeling.
- It laid the foundation for later advances in NLP and large language models.
- The Transformer became one of the most influential architectures in modern AI.
